In Ecuador, it inhabits the tropical humid Amazon rainforest in the provinces of Orellana, Pastaza, and Napo.

It is classified on Ecuador’s Red List of Amphibians under the category Least Concern (Criterion A2d), and on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species as Least Concern.

More information : https://amq.aiqua.it/index.php/amq/article/view/112

name: Scelidosaurus V2
description: Scelidosaurus was an early herbivorous dinosaur that lived during the Early Jurassic period, around 200 to 190 million years ago. Measuring about 4.5 meters (15 feet) in length, it was one of the earliest known armored dinosaurs, featuring rows of bony plates and spikes along its back and tail for defense. Scelidosaurus had a low, broad body with a relatively small head and a beak-like mouth, adapted for consuming low-lying vegetation. Its fossils have been found in what is now the United Kingdom, providing important insights into the evolution of ankylosaurs and their adaptations.

name: Costas Argyrou Museum - Owl or Thoupos 1980
description: Owls or thoupia were featured in his solo exhibitions in 1980, 1984, and 1992. The works Thoupos (88) and Owl I, mother of Owl II and III (89), made of porous stone from Skarinou, are the oldest and bear deeper engravings than the later works on the same theme. The work Owl I was included among the pieces with which he participated in the 1981 International Exhibition of Small Sculpture in Budapest, where he (Costas Argyrou) received one of the honorary diplomas. Later, in 1985, he created two more owls (90 and 91) from limestone, clarifying that they are the children of the first. Around the same time, he also created the work Owl IV (92). The work Koukouvaouthkia I (93), presented in his 1984 solo exhibition, and Koukouvaouthkia II (94), depict — the former — a group of three, and — the latter — a group of two small owls.

**Triceratops ignifrons: A Landmark Ceratopsid Discovery in Alberta**

In 2022, paleontologist Dr. Miriam Solano uncovered a striking ceratopsid specimen in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation of Alberta, Canada. Named *Triceratops ignifrons*—“Fire-Frilled Three-Horned Face”—this quadrupedal herbivore measured over 9 meters in length and featured an unusually elaborate frill with spiked margins and preserved pigment structures.

Spectroscopic analysis revealed traces of structural coloration, suggesting vivid blue, orange, and red hues across its frill and flanks. This challenges prior assumptions that ceratopsids relied solely on size and horn morphology for display. The discovery of *T. ignifrons* provides compelling evidence for visual signaling in herbivorous dinosaurs and deepens our understanding of social behavior and predator deterrence in Late Cretaceous ecosystems.

It inhabits rivers, lakes, and mangrove swamps where spends most the day in water to stay cool and hydrated. Just before night begins, they leave the water to forage on land.
